channel.title: Pickleball du Jour: tip of the day
channel.description: Simple, practical, ready for your next game. Plus complete guides to the rules, gear and tournaments in France and worldwide.

item.title: In singles, return deep and move up
item.description:
In singles, you cover the whole court alone. A deep return gives you time to reach the net before the server's third shot.

The two-bounce rule applies in singles too: the server has to let your return bounce. If it lands near their baseline, they hit from far back and you have time to move forward. A short return does the opposite: they move up, and you're still at the back when they attack.

Aim for their backhand corner, with some margin inside the lines. Then go all the way to the kitchen line without stopping halfway.

Once there, don't stand dead center. Shift one step toward the side you hit to, because their shortest passing shot goes down that line.

Try this: With a partner serving, hit twenty returns. Count how many bounce in the last two metres, then how many times you reach the kitchen line before their third shot crosses the net. Goal: 12 out of 20 in each count.

Read the tip

item.title: Serve deep, not hard
item.description:
A serve landing near the baseline pushes the receiver back and buys you time. Depth matters more than pace.

You only get one serve. Missing it hands over the serve. So aim for a big zone about three feet inside the opponent's baseline rather than for the lines.

A deep serve forces the receiver back. Their return will be shorter, and your third shot easier.

Try this: Put a towel three feet inside the far baseline. Ten serves: how many land beyond it?

Read the tip

item.title: After the return, get to the kitchen
item.description:
The receiving team has an edge: it can move to the net right after the return. Don't waste it by staying back.

Thanks to the two-bounce rule, the server must let your return bounce. Use that time to move forward. Hit your return deep and slow: it gives you more time to reach the kitchen line.

Stop just behind the line, feet apart, paddle in front.

Try this: Hit ten returns and count your steps to the kitchen line out loud. Goal: be there before the ball comes back over the net.

Read the tip

item.title: The third shot is the drop
item.description:
The serving team is stuck at the back. A drop, a soft ball into the opponent's kitchen, lets it move up without being punished.

Drive your third shot at opponents already at the net and it'll come back at your feet. The drop forces them to play a low ball they can't attack.

Aim just over the net with a soft arc, and take two or three steps forward as soon as it leaves your paddle.

Try this: From the baseline, hit twenty drops into the opponent's kitchen. Count how many bounce there.

Read the tip

item.title: Paddle up, always
item.description:
At the net, exchanges are too fast to bring your paddle up from your waist. Keep it in front, at chest height.

It's the number one beginner habit: the paddle drops after every shot. So you're always late on speed-ups.

Ready position: paddle in front of your chest, head slightly up, elbows in front of your body. Come back to it after every shot.

Try this: During a game, ask your partner to shout "paddle" every time yours drops below your waist.

Read the tip

item.title: Dinking is patience
item.description:
A dink rally is rarely won by a brilliant shot. It's won when the other side loses patience and pops the ball up.

The point of a dink isn't to win the rally but to give your opponent a ball they can't attack: low, in the kitchen, ideally to their backhand.

Wait for the ball that's too high. That one you can speed up.

Try this: Dink rally with a partner: first to hit outside the kitchen or into the net loses the point. Play to 11.

Read the tip

item.title: Three words that save a doubles game
item.description:
"Mine", "yours", "leave it". In doubles, half the points lost down the middle come from silence.

The ball down the middle is the most dangerous: each player thinks the other has it. Agree before the match. Often, the player with the forehand in the middle takes it.

And shout "leave it" when a ball is going out. Your partner doesn't always have time to judge.

Try this: Play a game where every middle ball must be called out loud. Fault if nobody speaks.

Read the tip

item.title: Watch your momentum after a volley
item.description:
Volley just in front of the line, then step into the kitchen, even after the rally ends: that's a fault. Momentum counts.

It's the most frustrating fault: the winning volley, then the foot sliding into the kitchen. The French federation tightened this rule in September 2026.

Stay slightly back from the line to volley, and brake before you hit, not after.

Try this: Volley with a partner and freeze after each shot. Feet still before the next contact.

Read the tip

item.title: Aim at the feet, not the head
item.description:
A ball arriving at a net player's feet is almost impossible to return aggressively.

When you speed up, the temptation is to hit at chest height. But a high ball is easy to volley. A low ball at the shoes forces a defensive half-volley.

Try this: Lay a paddle on the ground in front of your partner's feet and aim at it for ten speed-ups.

Read the tip

item.title: Five minutes of warm-up
item.description:
Pickleball injuries mostly hit ankles, calves and shoulders. Five minutes are enough to prevent most of them.

Before playing: brisk walking, high knees, side shuffles, shoulder and wrist rotations. Then a few easy dinks before speeding up.

Lateral movement and sudden stops are what load the body most.

Try this: Before your next session: 1 minute of side shuffles, 1 minute of shoulder rotations, 3 minutes of dinks.

Read the tip

item.title: Call the score out loud
item.description:
In doubles, the score has three numbers and everyone gets lost. Calling it before each serve prevents arguments.

The server calls their score, then the opponents', then their server number: "4-2-1". The game starts at "0-0-2".

Tip: when your team's score is even, your team's first server should be on the right. If not, something's wrong.

Try this: For a whole game, each player calls the score when it's their turn to serve.

Read the tip

item.title: Dink to the backhand
item.description:
For most players the backhand is weaker, especially at the net. Send your dinks there.

Spot who's right- and left-handed during the warm-up. In doubles, the diagonal to a right-hander's backhand is often the most comfortable to attack.

Try this: During a dink rally, play only to your partner's backhand. They must keep the ball low.

Read the tip

item.title: Lob, but rarely
item.description:
A good lob is beautiful. A short lob is a gift-wrapped smash. Keep it as a surprise.

The lob works against opponents glued to the kitchen line and leaning forward. It fails in wind or when the opponent is already backing up.

Outdoors with the wind behind you, forget it.

Try this: Hit five lobs in practice and note how many truly land behind the opponent's service line.

Read the tip

item.title: Learn the reset
item.description:
Under pressure, don't counterattack: slow down. A soft ball into the kitchen puts everyone back on equal terms.

When an opponent speeds up at you mid-court, the best answer is often a soft ball, open paddle, dying in the kitchen. That's a reset.

The secret: a loose grip and a short motion that absorbs pace instead of returning it.

Try this: Your partner at the net speeds up at you from the kitchen. You, mid-court, send every ball back into their kitchen.

Read the tip

item.title: Use the right ball
item.description:
Outdoor ball indoors: it bounces too much and skids. Indoor ball outdoors: the wind takes it.

Outdoor balls are heavier and harder, with more, smaller holes. Indoor balls are lighter and softer. They have 26 to 40 holes depending on the model.

In sanctioned play, the ball must be on the USA Pickleball approved list.

Try this: If you play in both conditions, keep a tube of each in your bag and label which is which.

Read the tip

item.title: One grip for everything
item.description:
The "hammer", or continental, grip lets you play forehand, backhand and volley without changing grip.

Hold the paddle like a hammer, edge towards the net. At the net, you'll never have time to switch grips between volleys.

Don't squeeze: on a scale of 1 to 10, stay around 4.

Try this: Play a whole dink session holding the hammer grip, never adjusting it.

Read the tip

item.title: Don't stay mid-court
item.description:
The area between the baseline and the kitchen, the transition zone, is where balls land at your feet. Move through it.

After the third shot, move up in stages: hit, step in, split-step as your opponent hits, then go again. Aim to reach the kitchen line in two or three shots.

Try this: From the baseline, try to reach the kitchen in three shots max while your partner feeds you low balls.

Read the tip

item.title: Move as if you're tied together
item.description:
In doubles, picture a ten-foot rope between you and your partner. When one moves, the other follows.

If your partner is pulled wide, slide to the middle to close the gap. If you move up, move up together. A staggered team, one up and one back, opens a highway down the diagonal.

Try this: Play a game where you must keep your partner beside you, never in front or behind.

Read the tip

item.title: Speed up the right ball
item.description:
A speed-up at the wrong moment comes back faster than it left. Wait for a ball above the net.

In a dink rally, don't speed up a low ball: you'd have to hit upwards, and your opponent just volleys down.

The right ball to speed up arrives at hip height or higher.

Try this: During a dink rally, only speed up balls that clear the top of the net by more than eight inches.

Read the tip

item.title: Play the wind
item.description:
Wind behind you: play shorter and softer. Wind in your face: you can hit harder, the ball will be slowed.

The pickleball is light and perforated: wind carries it far more than a tennis ball. At every change of ends, recalibrate.

Try this: At the warm-up, hit five dinks each way to feel the wind before the first point.

Read the tip

item.title: One point at a time
item.description:
Only the serving team scores: you can lose six rallies without losing a point. Don't panic.

Pickleball's scoring system is your friend in tough moments. As long as your opponent doesn't serve well, they don't score. Focus on the current rally, not the score.

Try this: After each lost point, take one slow breath before resetting. Three seconds, no more.

Read the tip

item.title: The erne, for bold players
item.description:
Going around the kitchen to volley from outside the court is legal, as long as you don't touch the zone.

When an opponent dinks along the sideline, you can jump over the corner of the kitchen, or set up outside the court beside it, to volley. Surprise guaranteed.

Condition: your feet must not touch the kitchen or its lines, before or during the shot.

Try this: In practice, walk slowly past the kitchen five times without a ball to memorise where to put your feet.

Read the tip

item.title: Beginner? Go light
item.description:
A 7 to 8 oz paddle forgives mistakes and protects your elbow. You can move to heavier later.

Heavy paddles add power, but in pickleball control wins points. And a tired arm misses dinks.

Expect €45 to €85 for a good first paddle.

Try this: Before buying, test two paddles of different weights at your club, at least twenty minutes each.

Read the tip

item.title: When in doubt, go middle
item.description:
A ball between the two opponents creates hesitation and cuts the angles they can send back.

Aiming at the sidelines is risky: little margin, and the opponent can reply with an angle. The middle is safe, and it's often where confusion starts on the other side.

Try this: For one game, hit every attacking ball down the middle. Count the errors it causes.

Read the tip

item.title: Shoes before the paddle
item.description:
Pickleball means lateral movement and sudden stops. Running shoes are a sprain waiting to happen.

Get court shoes: tennis or padel outdoors, indoor court shoes inside. Good ankle support and a sole that grips without sticking.

Try this: Check your current soles: if they're smooth or heavily rounded at the sides, replace them before your next session.

Read the tip
